events.title: Early Hunter-Gatherers
events.description: The earliest evidence of human habitation in the Lesotho region dates back to the Stone Age. The San people (Bushmen) were the earliest known inhabitants of the area, living as hunter-gatherers and leaving behind rich rock art in mountain caves. These paintings depict animals, hunting scenes, and ritual activities, representing one of the most important prehistoric art heritages in southern Africa. Lesotho's highlands provided shelter and abundant wildlife resources for these early inhabitants.

events.title: Bantu Migration Begins
events.description: Bantu-speaking peoples began migrating southward from Central and East Africa into southern Africa. These early Bantu brought iron-working technology, agricultural knowledge, and pastoralism. They began interacting with the local San people, sometimes coexisting peacefully and sometimes in conflict. The arrival of Bantu speakers marked a transition from hunter-gatherer societies to agricultural societies in the region.

events.title: Iron Age Development
events.description: Bantu-speaking peoples established more permanent settlements in the Lesotho region, with iron-working technology becoming widespread. Archaeological evidence shows the emergence of specialized blacksmiths who crafted agricultural tools, weapons, and implements. Pottery making also became more sophisticated, displaying distinctive regional styles. These communities began cultivating sorghum, millet, and other crops while raising cattle, sheep, and goats. Population gradually increased, village sizes expanded, and social division of labor became more pronounced.

events.title: Early Sotho Culture Emergence
events.description: The cultural characteristics of Sotho-speaking groups began to form distinctly, differentiating from other Bantu-speaking groups. Communities of this period developed unique architectural styles, constructing circular houses using stone and mud with grass or reed thatched roofs. Social organization was based on patrilineal clans, with chiefly power transmitted through heredity. Cattle continued to occupy a central position in economic and social life, used for marriage exchanges, ritual sacrifices, and symbols of social status. Trade connections with the eastern coast and northern regions began to establish.

events.title: Clan Territorial Expansion
events.description: Multiple Sotho-speaking clans expanded their territories in the mountainous and highland areas of present-day Lesotho, establishing more settlements. Complex political relationships formed between different clans, including alliances, tributary relationships, and competition. Chiefs expanded their influence through marriage alliances, military power, and diplomatic skills. During this period, rainmaking rituals and ancestor veneration became important religious practices. Traditional oral histories and praise poems (lithoko) began to develop, recording clan origins and important events.

events.title: Sotho-Tswana Settlement
events.description: Sotho-Tswana speaking Bantu groups established settlements in present-day Lesotho and surrounding areas. These groups included various clans and chiefdoms who lived by agriculture and pastoralism, particularly cattle herding. Cattle held important economic and social significance in Sotho culture, serving as symbols of wealth, status, and bride price. These early communities developed complex social structures led by hereditary chiefs.

events.title: Basotho Clan Formation
events.description: Multiple Sotho-speaking clans settled and developed in the Lesotho highlands, including the Bakoena, Bataung, Bafokeng and others. These clans were independent, ruled by their own chiefs and controlling specific territories. They developed lifestyles adapted to the highland environment, including terrace agriculture and highland pastoralism. Clans engaged in both trade and territorial disputes with each other.

events.title: Birth of Moshoeshoe I
events.description: Moshoeshoe I was born at Menkhoaneng in present-day Lesotho, originally named Lepoqo. He was born into a minor chief's family of the Bakoena clan. From youth, Moshoeshoe displayed leadership abilities and diplomatic wisdom, qualities that later made him the founder and greatest leader of the Basotho nation. His name 'Moshoeshoe' means 'the shaver,' reportedly because he shaved off enemies' beards as swiftly as a razor during a raid.

events.title: Difaqane Period of Turmoil
events.description: Southern Africa experienced the Difaqane (Mfecane, meaning 'crushing' or 'forced migration'), a period of cascading wars and population movements triggered by Zulu King Shaka's military expansion. This turmoil caused massive violence, famine, and population displacement. Many clans were destroyed or forced to migrate, plunging the entire region into chaos. This period of upheaval created conditions for Moshoeshoe I's rise.

events.title: Establishment of Butha-Buthe Fortress
events.description: Facing chaos and threats during the Difaqane period, Moshoeshoe I made the crucial decision to move his followers to Butha-Buthe mountain. This easily defensible mountain fortress provided safe refuge for his people. Moshoeshoe began accepting refugees from various war-torn clans, regardless of origin, as long as they acknowledged his leadership. This inclusive policy was key to his success and the beginning of Basotho nation formation.

events.title: Resistance Against Matabele and Nguni Raids
events.description: Moshoeshoe's fortress was repeatedly attacked by powerful Matabele warriors and other Nguni groups. Moshoeshoe successfully repelled these attacks using clever defensive strategies and diplomacy. He relied not only on military defense but also avoided unnecessary conflict through paying tribute and building alliances. These experiences honed Basotho fighting capabilities and established Moshoeshoe's reputation as a wise leader.

events.title: Migration to Thaba Bosiu
events.description: Moshoeshoe I moved his capital to the more formidable Thaba Bosiu mountain (meaning 'Mountain of Night'). This flat-topped mountain stands about 1,800 meters above sea level, surrounded by steep cliffs with only a few narrow passages to the summit, making it an ideal natural fortress. Legend says the mountain grows taller at night, preventing enemies from climbing it. Thaba Bosiu became the heart of the Basotho kingdom, never conquered during Moshoeshoe's reign, and a symbol of the Basotho nation.

events.title: Arrival of French Missionaries
events.description: French missionaries from the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society arrived in Basutoland, led by Eugène Casalis, Thomas Arbousset, and Constant Gosselin. Moshoeshoe I welcomed these missionaries, seeing strategic value in establishing connections with Europeans. The missionaries not only spread Christianity but also introduced literacy, modern agricultural techniques, and European diplomatic knowledge. Casalis became Moshoeshoe's close advisor and translator, providing diplomatic support at crucial moments.

events.title: Establishment of Morija Mission
events.description: French missionaries established Morija mission station near Thaba Bosiu, which became one of Lesotho's most important religious, educational, and cultural centers. Morija developed a printing press, publishing the first Sesotho Bible and other books, making significant contributions to Sesotho language and literature development. The mission also established schools, training the first generation of Western-educated Basotho. Morija remains an important part of Lesotho's cultural heritage today.

events.title: First Conflicts with Boers
events.description: Boers (Dutch-descended South Africans) from the Cape Colony began the Great Trek, moving inland seeking new lands. Boers started encroaching on Basotho traditional grazing lands and farmlands, triggering first conflicts. Moshoeshoe attempted to resolve disputes through diplomacy, but Boer expansion pressure became the main threat to the Basotho kingdom. This marked the beginning of long-term conflict between Basotho and European colonizers.

events.title: British Annexation of Orange River Sovereignty
events.description: Britain annexed the region north of the Orange River, establishing the Orange River Sovereignty and bringing Basutoland into British sphere of influence. British Governor Harry Smith attempted to demarcate boundaries between Boers and Basotho. Moshoeshoe initially welcomed British protection, hoping it would curb Boer expansion. However, British-drawn boundaries disadvantaged the Basotho, depriving them of large tracts of fertile land.

events.title: War with Britain
events.description: Due to dissatisfaction with British-drawn boundaries and British attempts to disarm the Basotho, Moshoeshoe came into conflict with Britain. In 1851, the British Governor launched an attack on Thaba Bosiu but was repelled by the Basotho. In 1852, both sides signed a peace treaty, with Britain recognizing Moshoeshoe's independent status and control over most territories. This victory enhanced Moshoeshoe's prestige and proved Basotho military strength.

events.title: Establishment of Orange Free State
events.description: Britain abandoned the Orange River Sovereignty, and Boers established the independent Orange Free State Republic. This was a catastrophic development for the Basotho, as Boers were more aggressive than the British and more eager to seize Basotho lands. The Orange Free State shared a long border with the Basotho kingdom, and border conflicts became frequent and intense. This set the stage for decades of warfare.

events.title: First Basotho-Boer War
events.description: The Orange Free State launched the first large-scale war against Basutoland, attempting to seize fertile Caledon Valley lands. The war lasted several months with both sides suffering significant losses. The Basotho used mountain terrain for guerrilla warfare, successfully resisting Boer attacks. The war ended with a peace treaty, but border issues remained unresolved, laying groundwork for future conflicts.

events.title: Second Basotho-Boer War
events.description: The Orange Free State again launched war against the Basotho, this time more intense and brutal. Boers equipped with more advanced weapons conducted devastating raids on Basotho villages, destroying crops and livestock, attempting to starve the Basotho. Despite valiant Basotho resistance, they gradually fell into disadvantage. The war caused enormous casualties and economic losses, with the Basotho kingdom facing a survival crisis.

events.title: Treaty of Thaba Bosiu
events.description: At the end of the Second Basotho-Boer War, both sides signed the Treaty of Thaba Bosiu. This was an extremely unfavorable treaty for the Basotho, forcing Moshoeshoe to cede large tracts of fertile western lowlands, including important agricultural areas. The Basotho lost about 40% of arable land and large numbers of livestock. This territorial loss had long-term impacts on the Basotho economy, forcing many Basotho to live in more barren highlands.

events.title: Third Basotho-Boer War
events.description: Unsatisfied with gains from the Treaty of Thaba Bosiu, the Orange Free State launched war again, attempting to completely conquer Basutoland. This war was a desperate struggle for the Basotho, facing danger of complete annihilation. Boer attacks were more fierce, and Basotho resistance became increasingly difficult. Moshoeshoe realized that without external help, the Basotho kingdom could not survive.

events.title: Becoming British Protectorate
events.description: Facing continued Orange Free State aggression and survival threats, Moshoeshoe I requested protection from British Queen Victoria. On March 12, 1868, Britain declared Basutoland a British protectorate, called Basutoland. This decision saved the Basotho nation from Boer conquest and annexation. Though losing independence, the Basotho retained their land, culture, and traditional leadership structures. This day later became Lesotho's national day (Moshoeshoe Day).

events.title: Treaty of Aliwal North
events.description: Britain and the Orange Free State signed the Treaty of Aliwal North, formally determining Basutoland's boundaries. However, this treaty confirmed large territories the Basotho lost in previous wars, including the fertile 'Conquered Territory.' These lands later became part of the Orange Free State, now part of South Africa's Free State province. Many Basotho still lived on these lost lands, becoming a minority in South Africa.

events.title: Death of Moshoeshoe I
events.description: Moshoeshoe I, founder and great leader of the Basotho nation, died at Thaba Bosiu aged about 84. His death marked the end of an era. Through his wisdom, diplomatic skills, and military talent, Moshoeshoe united scattered Sotho clans into a unified nation during the turbulent 19th century and ensured their survival. He was buried atop Thaba Bosiu, and his grave remains Lesotho's most sacred place. Moshoeshoe is revered as 'Father of the Nation,' and his legacy deeply influences modern Lesotho.

events.title: Succession Crisis and Internal Conflicts
events.description: After Moshoeshoe I's death, his son Letsie I succeeded, but the kingdom fell into succession disputes and internal conflicts. Multiple sons and grandsons of Moshoeshoe competed for power and territory, leading to division and weakening of the Basotho kingdom. British colonial authorities exploited these internal divisions to strengthen control over Basutoland. The traditional chieftaincy system was challenged, and central authority weakened.

events.title: Annexation to Cape Colony
events.description: Britain transferred Basutoland from direct imperial rule to Cape Colony jurisdiction. The Cape Colony government began implementing more direct rule over Basutoland, attempting to weaken traditional chiefs' power and introduce European-style legal and administrative systems. This change caused Basotho discontent as they felt their autonomy was being eroded.

events.title: Gun War
events.description: The Cape Colony government attempted to disarm the Basotho, enacting the Peace Preservation Act requiring Basotho to surrender their guns and horses. The Basotho strongly opposed this, as guns were crucial for their survival, hunting, and self-defense. In 1880, the Basotho launched armed uprising under Chief Letsie I and his sons, known as the 'Gun War' or 'Basutoland Rebellion.' The Basotho used mountain terrain for guerrilla warfare, successfully resisting Cape Colony military attacks.

events.title: Gun War Victory
events.description: After over a year of fighting, the Cape Colony government realized it could not militarily conquer the Basotho and was forced to negotiate. A peace treaty was signed in 1881, allowing the Basotho to keep their weapons. This was a major Basotho victory, proving their determination to resist and fighting capability. The Gun War became an important source of Basotho national pride and one of Africa's successful cases of resistance against colonial rule.

events.title: Return to British Crown Colony Status
events.description: Due to Gun War failure and difficulties managing Basutoland, Britain removed Basutoland from Cape Colony jurisdiction, placing it again under direct British rule as a Crown Colony. This change was positive for the Basotho, as Britain adopted a more indirect rule approach, governing through traditional chiefs and preserving more local autonomy. Basutoland became one of the few regions in southern Africa that retained most traditional institutions.

events.title: Beginning of Labor Migration
events.description: With development of South African gold and diamond mines, large numbers of Basotho men began working in South African mines as migrant laborers. This labor migration pattern had profound impacts on Basutoland's economy and society. Remittances became the main income source for many families, but also led to family separation, agricultural labor shortages, and social structure changes. This pattern of dependence on external labor markets continues today.

events.title: Expansion of Morija Printing Press
events.description: The printing press at Morija mission station expanded significantly, beginning publication of the Sesotho newspaper 'Leselinyana' (meaning 'The Little Light'). This newspaper became an important source of information and cultural expression platform for the Basotho, reporting local news, publishing commentary articles, and promoting literacy. The press also published Sesotho textbooks, religious literature, and historical works, making tremendous contributions to the development of Sesotho written culture. This marked the beginning of modern media and publishing industry in Basutoland.

events.title: Establishment of Basutoland National Council
events.description: British colonial authorities established the Basutoland National Council as an advisory body, composed of traditional chiefs and some appointed members. Though the council had limited powers, mainly providing advice to the British Resident Commissioner, it provided a platform for Basotho political participation and was a prototype for future democratic institutions. The council discussed taxation, land use, education, and other local affairs.

events.title: South Africa Act Discussions
events.description: During British Parliament discussions of the South Africa Act, Basotho chiefs sent a delegation to London to strongly oppose Basutoland's incorporation into the soon-to-be-formed Union of South Africa. The delegation, led by representatives of Chief Letsie II, presented to the British government Basotho concerns about losing land, facing racial discrimination, and being deprived of self-governance. Though this lobbying was not immediately successful, it laid the groundwork for Basutoland's later maintenance of independent status.

events.title: Refusal to Join Union of South Africa
events.description: When Britain's four South African colonies (Cape, Natal, Transvaal, and Orange River) merged into the Union of South Africa, Basutoland, Bechuanaland (now Botswana), and Swaziland were excluded. Basotho leaders strongly opposed incorporation into South Africa, fearing loss of land and autonomy and oppression under South African apartheid policies. Britain agreed to retain these three territories as British protectorates, called 'High Commission Territories.' This decision was crucial for Lesotho's future.

events.title: Impact of South African Land Act
events.description: South Africa passed the Natives Land Act, severely restricting African people's ability to purchase and lease land. Though this law did not directly apply to Basutoland, it had profound impacts on the Basotho people. Many Basotho living in South Africa's 'Conquered Territory' lost their land rights and were forced to become tenant farmers or migrant laborers. This intensified Basotho fears of South African racial policies and strengthened their resolve to resist incorporation into South Africa. The law also increased the number of laborers migrating from Basutoland to work in South Africa.

events.title: Education Expansion and Mission Schools
events.description: Christian missions established more schools in Basutoland, significantly expanding educational opportunities. Besides the French mission, the Anglican Church, Roman Catholic Church, and other denominations also established school networks. These schools taught literacy, arithmetic, religious knowledge, and some vocational skills. By the late 1920s, Basutoland's literacy rate was relatively high in southern Africa. Educational expansion cultivated a new generation of Western-educated Basotho elites who later became leaders of the nationalist movement. Meanwhile, traditional education systems (such as initiation schools) continued to exist, creating a dual education system.

events.title: Soil Erosion Crisis
events.description: Due to population growth, overgrazing, and improper agricultural practices, Basutoland began facing severe soil erosion problems. Hillside vegetation was destroyed, leading to massive soil loss and formation of deep gullies (dongas). This environmental crisis threatened Basutoland's agricultural foundation and long-term viability. Colonial authorities attempted to implement soil conservation measures, but with limited effect. Soil erosion remains a major environmental challenge for Lesotho today.

events.title: Basotho Participation in World War II
events.description: As World War II approached, many Basotho men voluntarily joined British forces or served in South African military units. Though Basutoland was not directly involved in the war, thousands of Basotho fought in North Africa, Italy, and other battlefields. Their wartime experiences broadened their horizons and exposed them to democratic and freedom ideals; many returned home after the war bringing back anti-colonial ideas. During the war, Basutoland's economy was also affected by providing food and labor to the Allied forces.

events.title: Rise of Nationalist Movement
events.description: Influenced by post-WWII global decolonization wave, modern nationalist movements began emerging in Basutoland. Educated Basotho elites began demanding more political rights and autonomy. They criticized the conservatism of the traditional chieftaincy system and called for establishing modern democratic institutions. This period saw the emergence of first political organizations and newspapers, laying foundations for future independence movements.

events.title: Formation of Basutoland Congress Party
events.description: Ntsu Mokhehle and other nationalists formed the Basutoland Congress Party (BCP), Basutoland's first modern political party. The party demanded immediate independence, opposed traditional chiefs' power, and advocated establishing a democratic republic. The BCP was influenced by pan-Africanism and socialist ideas, attracting support from youth and intellectuals.

events.title: Formation of Basutoland National Party
events.description: Chief Leabua Jonathan formed the Basutoland National Party (BNP) as political representative of conservatives and traditional chiefs. The party supported cooperation with traditional institutions, adopted a more moderate independence approach, and maintained friendly relations with South Africa. The BNP gained support from the Catholic Church and some chiefs, becoming the main competitor to the BCP.

events.title: Constitutional Reform and Elections
events.description: Britain began promoting constitutional reform in Basutoland, introducing a new constitution that expanded National Council powers and introduced an electoral system. The first district council elections were held in 1960. Though voting rights remained limited, this marked an important step toward democratic institutions in Basutoland. Political parties began mobilizing the public, and political competition intensified.

events.title: First General Election
events.description: Basutoland held its first comprehensive pre-independence general election, the first election based on universal suffrage in southern Africa. Election results were surprising, with the Basutoland National Party under Leabua Jonathan winning, defeating the widely favored BCP. Jonathan became Chief Minister, leading the self-governing government. Election results reflected rural voters' support for traditional values and cautious attitude toward radical change.

events.title: Lesotho Independence
events.description: Basutoland formally gained independence from Britain, renamed the Kingdom of Lesotho. Moshoeshoe II (great-grandson of Moshoeshoe I) became King, and Leabua Jonathan became first Prime Minister. Independence celebrations were held in capital Maseru, marking Lesotho's emergence as a sovereign state. However, Lesotho faced enormous challenges: economic backwardness, complete encirclement by South Africa, political division, and environmental degradation.

events.title: Election Crisis and Coup
events.description: Lesotho held its first post-independence general election, with preliminary results showing the opposition BCP would win. Prime Minister Leabua Jonathan refused to accept election results, declared the election invalid, suspended the constitution, and staged a coup to seize power. He arrested opposition leaders and exiled King Moshoeshoe II (later allowing him to return in a ceremonial role). Jonathan established authoritarian rule, interrupting Lesotho's democratic process. This coup opened a period of long-term political instability in Lesotho.

events.title: Complex Relations with South Africa
events.description: Jonathan's government initially maintained friendly relations with South Africa's apartheid regime but shifted in the mid-1970s, criticizing apartheid and allowing South African ANC exiles to seek refuge in Lesotho. This led to South African economic and military pressure on Lesotho, including border blockades and support for Lesotho opposition. Lesotho's economy was highly dependent on South Africa, placing it in an extremely vulnerable position.

events.title: Formation of Lesotho Liberation Army
events.description: Exiled BCP leader Ntsu Mokhehle formed the Lesotho Liberation Army (LLA) with Libyan support, beginning armed struggle against Jonathan's regime. The LLA launched attacks from South Africa and Mozambique, aiming to overthrow Jonathan's government. This plunged Lesotho into low-intensity civil war, exacerbating political instability and violence.

events.title: Military Coup
events.description: The Lesotho Defense Force under Major General Justin Lekhanya staged a military coup, overthrowing Leabua Jonathan's 16-year government. The coup was conducted with South African support and pressure, as South Africa wanted a more compliant regime. The military government dissolved parliament, banned political party activities, and restored some powers to King Moshoeshoe II. However, relations between the military government and the King quickly deteriorated.

events.title: King Dethroned
events.description: Power struggle between military government leader Lekhanya and King Moshoeshoe II escalated. In 1990, Lekhanya forced Moshoeshoe II to abdicate and go into exile, installing Moshoeshoe's son Letsie III as new King. This action drew widespread domestic and international criticism, viewed as violation of traditional monarchy. Moshoeshoe II continued to receive support from many Basotho during exile.

events.title: Lekhanya Overthrown
events.description: Justin Lekhanya was overthrown in another military coup, with a military council led by Colonel Phisoane Ramaema taking power. The new military government promised to restore democracy and began dialogue with political parties and civil society organizations. This marked the beginning of Lesotho's transition to democracy, though the process was full of challenges and setbacks.

events.title: Restoration of Democratic Elections
events.description: Under military government supervision, Lesotho held its first free elections since 1970. The BCP under Ntsu Mokhehle won an overwhelming victory, capturing all 65 parliamentary seats. Mokhehle became Prime Minister, and the military government peacefully transferred power. This election was seen as an important milestone in Lesotho's democratization, ending 23 years of authoritarian rule.

events.title: Restoration of Moshoeshoe II
events.description: Under domestic and international pressure, Letsie III agreed to step aside for his father Moshoeshoe II, who returned from exile and resumed the throne. This decision was widely welcomed, viewed as restoration of tradition and legitimacy. Moshoeshoe II's restoration helped stabilize the political situation, though his powers remained largely ceremonial.

events.title: BCP Split
events.description: The ruling BCP experienced serious internal split, with power struggle erupting between Prime Minister Mokhehle and Deputy Prime Minister Molapo Qhobela. Qhobela and other dissatisfied party members broke away from the BCP, forming the new Lesotho Congress for Democracy (LCD). This split led to political instability and set the stage for future electoral crises.

events.title: Death of Moshoeshoe II in Car Accident
events.description: King Moshoeshoe II died in a suspicious car accident aged 57. His death sparked conspiracy theories and speculation, with many suspecting it was not an accident. Moshoeshoe's son Letsie III again inherited the throne. Moshoeshoe II's death was a major loss for Lesotho, as he was viewed as a symbol of national unity and guardian of tradition.

events.title: Attempted Military Mutiny
events.description: Some officers of the Lesotho Defense Force staged a mutiny, demanding higher wages and better conditions. The mutiny was suppressed by the government but exposed discontent and discipline problems within the military. This incident revealed the fragility of Lesotho's security sector and the military's continued influence in politics.

events.title: Controversial Election
events.description: Lesotho held general elections, with the newly formed LCD under Pakalitha Mosisili winning an overwhelming victory, capturing 79 of 80 seats. Opposition parties alleged electoral fraud and refused to accept results. Political tensions rapidly escalated, leading to mass protests and violence. The country plunged into political crisis, threatening democratic institutions' survival.

events.title: SADC Military Intervention
events.description: As political crisis worsened and military mutiny threatened, Lesotho's government requested SADC intervention. South Africa and Botswana sent troops into Lesotho to 'restore law and order.' The intervention met fierce resistance, leading to violent clashes and widespread looting and destruction, with much of Maseru's commercial district burned. The intervention stabilized the situation short-term but also caused significant economic losses and political trauma.

events.title: Political Reform and Interim Political Authority
events.description: Under SADC mediation, Lesotho's political parties agreed to political reforms to prevent future electoral crises. The Interim Political Authority (IPA) was established, composed of representatives from various parties, responsible for overseeing electoral system reform and preparing new elections. The core reform was introducing Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) representation to ensure opposition party representation in parliament.

events.title: First Election Under New Electoral System
events.description: Lesotho held elections under the new MMP system. The LCD won again, but opposition parties also gained parliamentary seats. The new system was considered more fair and inclusive, helping reduce political tensions. Pakalitha Mosisili continued as Prime Minister, beginning a relatively stable governing period.

events.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project Corruption Scandal
events.description: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project (LHWP), one of Africa's largest infrastructure projects designed to supply water to South Africa and generate electricity for Lesotho, became embroiled in a massive corruption scandal. Multiple international companies were accused of bribing Lesotho officials to secure contracts. LHWP Chief Executive Masupha Sole was convicted and imprisoned. This scandal exposed corruption in Lesotho's government and damaged the country's international reputation.

events.title: LCD Split Again
events.description: The ruling LCD experienced another internal split, with 17 MPs breaking away to form the All Basotho Convention (ABC). This split was due to dissatisfaction with Prime Minister Mosisili's leadership style and policies. The ABC, led by former Foreign Minister Thomas Thabane, quickly became the main opposition party.

events.title: Snap Election
events.description: Due to ruling party split causing loss of parliamentary majority, Lesotho held snap elections. The LCD won again but with reduced margin. The newly formed ABC performed strongly, becoming the main opposition party. The election process was relatively peaceful, viewed as a positive sign of Lesotho's democratic consolidation.

events.title: Historic Coalition Government
events.description: Lesotho held general elections with no party winning absolute majority. After negotiations, the ABC, LCD (Mokhehle faction), and BNP formed a coalition government, with Thomas Thabane becoming Prime Minister. This was Lesotho's first coalition government and first peaceful transfer of power through elections. This was seen as an important sign of Lesotho's democratic maturity.

events.title: Coalition Government Collapse and Political Crisis
events.description: Serious divisions emerged within the coalition government, with relations between Prime Minister Thabane and Deputy Prime Minister Mosisili breaking down. Thabane accused Mosisili and military leaders of plotting a coup. Political tensions escalated, with Thabane suspending parliament to prevent a no-confidence vote. The country again plunged into political crisis, threatening democratic stability.

events.title: Military Conflict and Prime Minister's Flight
events.description: The Lesotho Defense Force attacked police headquarters and other security facilities, causing casualties. Prime Minister Thabane fled to South Africa, claiming his life was threatened and accusing the military of attempting a coup. This incident raised serious international concern, with SADC intervening to mediate. Lesotho again faced the brink of political collapse.

events.title: Snap Election and New Coalition Government
events.description: Under SADC mediation, Lesotho held snap elections to resolve the political crisis. The LCD won the most seats, with Pakalitha Mosisili again becoming Prime Minister, leading a new seven-party coalition government. The election process was relatively peaceful, but political divisions remained severe. The new government faced enormous challenges in restoring stability and promoting reform.

events.title: Political Assassinations and Instability
events.description: Lesotho experienced a series of political assassinations, including military commanders and political figures. These assassinations exacerbated political instability and atmosphere of fear. Prime Minister Mosisili was implicated in the 2017 murder of former army commander Maaparankoe Mahao, though he denied the charges. Political violence became a worrying feature of Lesotho politics.

events.title: Mosisili's Resignation
events.description: Facing pressure within the coalition government and threat of no-confidence vote, Prime Minister Pakalitha Mosisili announced his resignation. His resignation marked the end of his 15-year (in two terms) prime ministerial career. Mosisili was Lesotho's longest-serving prime minister, but his legacy was questioned due to corruption allegations and political instability.

events.title: Thabane Returns as Prime Minister
events.description: In snap elections following Mosisili's resignation, the ABC-led alliance won, with Thomas Thabane becoming Prime Minister for the second time. Thabane promised to fight corruption, promote economic development and political reform. However, his government quickly also fell into internal divisions and power struggles.

events.title: ABC Split
events.description: The ruling ABC experienced serious internal split, with Deputy Prime Minister Monyane Moleleki and other senior members breaking with Prime Minister Thabane. The split was due to power distribution, policy disagreements, and personal grudges. This split weakened government stability and set the stage for new political crisis.

events.title: Thabane's Resignation
events.description: Facing coalition government collapse, no-confidence vote, and murder charges (related to 2017 killing of his ex-wife), Prime Minister Thomas Thabane announced his resignation. His resignation ended three turbulent years in office. Thabane later fled to South Africa to avoid prosecution in the murder case, though he claimed the charges were political persecution.

events.title: Majoro Becomes Prime Minister
events.description: The ABC elected Moeketsi Majoro as new leader, and he became Lesotho's new Prime Minister. Majoro, an economist and former Finance Minister, was viewed as a technocrat rather than traditional politician. He promised to stabilize the political situation, improve the economy, and respond to the COVID-19 pandemic. However, his government also faced challenges from factional struggles within the ABC.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Impact
events.description: The COVID-19 pandemic had severe impacts on Lesotho. Lesotho was one of the last countries in the world to report COVID-19 cases, but the pandemic eventually spread. Lockdown measures further damaged the already fragile economy, particularly affecting the textile industry and tourism. Many Lesotho workers in South Africa lost jobs and returned home, exacerbating domestic economic pressure. The pandemic also exposed the fragility of Lesotho's healthcare system.

events.title: ABC Internal Struggles Intensify
events.description: Factional struggles within the ABC further intensified, with conflict between Prime Minister Majoro and Thabane faction becoming public. Thabane attempted to remotely control party affairs from South Africa, while Majoro tried to consolidate his power. This infighting weakened government effectiveness and led to political instability.

events.title: Snap Election
events.description: Due to coalition government collapse and political deadlock, Lesotho held snap elections. This was Lesotho's fifth election since 2012, reflecting the country's continued political instability. The election was highly competitive, with multiple parties and alliances participating. The election process was relatively peaceful, but results again produced a divided parliament.

events.title: Revolution for Prosperity Party Victory
events.description: In the October 2022 election, the newly formed Revolution for Prosperity (RFP) party won the most seats. The party was founded by businessman Sam Matekane, who promised to bring business experience to government, fight corruption, and create jobs. The RFP formed a coalition government with other small parties, with Matekane becoming Prime Minister. This was a major change in Lesotho politics, marking the end of traditional party dominance.

events.title: Matekane Government's Reform Agenda
events.description: Prime Minister Sam Matekane's government began promoting an ambitious reform agenda, focusing on economic development, attracting foreign investment, improving infrastructure, and fighting corruption. The government promised to reform the public sector, improving efficiency and transparency. Matekane's business background and non-traditional politician image brought new atmosphere to Lesotho politics, but he also faced enormous expectations and challenges.

events.title: Constitutional and Security Sector Reforms
events.description: Lesotho continued promoting long-delayed constitutional reform and security sector reform. These reforms aimed to address root causes of political instability, including limiting prime ministerial powers, reforming the electoral system, and restructuring the military and police. SADC continued supporting these reform processes. However, reforms faced resistance from vested interests and implementation challenges.

events.title: Mountain Kingdom's Challenges and Hope
events.description: Lesotho, as the 'Mountain Kingdom' and 'Kingdom in the Sky,' continues facing multiple challenges. Economically, Lesotho is highly dependent on South Africa, with main income sources including customs revenue, remittances, textile industry, and water exports. Unemployment is extremely high, especially youth unemployment, with serious poverty and inequality problems. Environmentally, soil erosion, climate change, and water resource management are major challenges. Politically, despite progress, instability and factional struggles persist. Socially, Lesotho faces one of the world's highest HIV/AIDS infection rates, along with tuberculosis and other health problems. However, Lesotho also has advantages: abundant water resources, unique cultural heritage, relatively high literacy rate, and vibrant civil society. The Lesotho people are known for their resilience, pride, and strong sense of national identity. The new government brings hope for change, but Lesotho's future depends on achieving political stability, economic diversification, and social development. As a landlocked country completely surrounded by South Africa, Lesotho's fate is closely tied to South Africa, but it insists on maintaining its sovereignty and unique identity.
